items_missed: Never got the customer's name. The call opened 'Hello, this is Alex winds moving. How can I help?' and closed 'Thank you, ma'am' — seven minutes, a full quote delivered, and no name, no email, no phone captured. There is no lead record to follow up on, which matters because the call ended on a callback promise.
No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — no roadmap, no timeframe, no confirmation. Straight from 'How can I help?' to 'Did you have a particular date in mind?'
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

No quote recap even though the customer opened with 'I wanted to get a more accurate quote for moving' — that phrasing signals an existing online/instant quote, and Alex never asked what she'd already been quoted or referenced anything on file.
Never asked about special considerations — long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns — on a move between two apartment complexes, where those are the norm, not the exception.

Never asked for a box count. The customer said 'I'll have the back boxes packed but if you can help me with loading up the boxes unloading them' — boxes are explicitly in scope for the crew and the volume was never established, which is a direct hit on the hours estimate.

Access concerns never probed. The customer volunteered the elevator ('I'm on the fourth floor') herself; Alex never asked about elevator reservation, COI requirements, loading-dock or parking access at either complex. Two apartment buildings and zero access questions.

Never asked the moving-stressor question — no 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?' The customer gave an opening ('I need to be out of my place by the twenty sixth but I wanted to keep a day in-hand just to kinda like go the cleaning') and it drew only 'Okay, good deal.'

Base hourly rate never stated. He quoted totals ($1,376 at six hours, $1,582 at seven) but never said what the Friday per-hour rate was — the customer would have to back into $206/hr herself. The Tuesday–Thursday tier was given as '$192 per hour' for a two-mover team, not framed per mover per hour.
What's-included list was partial: 'moving blanket, shrink wrap bands any disassemble reassembly' — no gas, no truck, no taxes, no insurance, no tools, no pads.

No Worries Damage Coverage was mis-branded and under-explained: 'all of our moves also do come with up to $2,000 evaluation coverage.' The $2,000 and the no-extra-charge landed, but the brand name never did, and neither did 'repair, replace, or reimburse' or the 60¢/lb baseline it's being compared against.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and this was a customer with a hard deadline ('I need to be out of my place by the twenty sixth'), which is the single best setup for that differentiator on this call.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch. 'You really just have a total of two charges to be mindful of' is close, but the explicit no-credit-card-fee / no-fuel-surcharge / no-assembly-fee list never came — and it was needed, because the trip fee was the one thing she pushed back on twice.

No sense-check anywhere in the clock or pricing explanation. The pricing block ran roughly 250 words uninterrupted with no 'does that make sense?' — the customer's only input across it was 'Mm-hmm, Mm-hmm.'
Mover and truck count only came out because the customer asked. 'Oh, wow. Okay... and is that with how many movers?' → 'That'd be with two movers.' Truck count was never stated at all.

Estimate padded past his own stated range without an accuracy path. He said the typical two-bedroom apartment runs 'three and a half to five and a half hours on average,' then landed the quote at 'closer to about six or seven hours' — an hour and a half above his own top end, justified as 'I wanna make sure I give you more of a conservative budget here.' Three flights at the unload is real, but the origin has an elevator and it's a sub-1,100 sqft two-bedroom with no packing. This is the exact conservative-padding pattern driving the 45–46% estimate-accuracy number.
Walk distance never asked or factored, on a move where both ends are multi-unit complexes.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors (school-bus reference or similar) used to make the hours feel concrete.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload.' This was the ideal call for it: she's self-packing, needs help only with furniture and boxes, and the new place is 'literally less than a mile away' — a carload tip would have been immediately actionable and would have answered her 'is that the best you can do?' better than a day-of-week discount did.

Zero booking attempt. The customer said 'let me check back with my husband and I'll give you a callback' and the entire response was 'Okay, sounds good. Thank you, ma'am.' No offer to hold the 25th, no 'want me to pencil that in?', no specific follow-up time.

No deposit required was never mentioned — the highest-cost miss on the call. 'Let me check back with my husband' is a commitment-risk objection, and 'there's no deposit, so locking the date costs you nothing and you can still change it' is the exact answer.
No email handoff at all — no confirmation email offered, no email address collected, no bolded-details framing, no 'reply with any corrections.'

The photo suggestion was left dangling. He said 'if you want like a more accurate estimate, the best thing that I would suggest is just like sending over photos' and then never told her where to send them, never got her email, and never circled back to it.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' and no hours or how-to-reach-us before hanging up.
Customer's name used zero times — short of the 3+ standard.
top_strength: Alexander's command of the clock and fee mechanics is the best thing on this call, and he volunteered detail most reps skip. In one pass he covered the minimum, the proration, and both ends of the billable window: 'after a two and a half hour minimum the clock is prorated to the nearest fifteen minute interval of actual time used. That billable time only begins whenever we actually arrive at the starting address, it does include the drive time between locations but if the movers they stop for a launch at a gas station... then they do make sure to pause your clock for you,' and then closed the loop on the back end — 'the time would officially end after they unload the last item from their truck into the new home and then just conduct a final walkthrough with you to make sure everything gets staged appropriately and nothing gets left behind on our truck.' That is trust-building specificity nobody asked him for. He also handled the two objections cleanly and without defensiveness. On 'is that the best you can do?' he didn't discount and didn't stall — he reframed to a lever the customer controls: 'if you have the flexibility that would afford you the lowest hourly rate,' then reran both scenarios live at $192/hour. And on the trip fee — 'the place is literally less than a mile away, is that $140 still applicable?' — he held the price and explained the actual basis instead of hedging: 'The trip fee isn't based on the distance like the drive time between the old home and the new home. It's based on the commute time from with an empty truck going to the new home, and then that empty truck coming back over.' The customer's reply was 'I see. Okay, understood.' That is a fee objection fully resolved.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Alexander did the hard part — a full quote, two objections handled, a satisfied customer — and then gave the sale away in the last fifteen seconds. 'Let me check back with my husband and I'll give you a callback' got 'Okay, sounds good.' The line he needed was: 'Absolutely, talk it over with him. One thing that'll help — there's no deposit and no card on file to book, so I can hold Friday the 25th for you right now at no cost, and if the two of you decide differently you just let me know. What's the best email for you? I'll send the confirmation with the rate, the hours, and the trip fee all laid out at the top so he can read it himself.' That single move does four things this call missed: it attempts the booking, it delivers the no-deposit differentiator, it captures the email and the handoff, and it puts the numbers in front of the actual second decision-maker instead of relying on her to relay them. Second priority: he has no lead record. No name, no email, no phone, seven minutes of work and a quote in the customer's head only — if she doesn't call back, this lead does not exist. Get the name in the first thirty seconds and the email before the pricing block, every call. Third, the Save Your Ass speech is a total zero on the most Save-Your-Ass-friendly call in the sample: she's packing her own boxes and moving less than a mile. 'Since you're right across the road, anything small and awkward — the loose stuff in drawers, closet odds and ends, the pictures off the walls — take a carload or two over yourself before we get there. Every trip like that comes straight off your clock. Does that make sense?' That is a better answer to 'is that the best you can do?' than the Tuesday-through-Thursday rate, because it saves her money on the date she actually needs. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: he quoted 6–7 hours after stating the typical two-bedroom range is 3.5–5.5, explicitly calling it 'a more conservative budget.' Three flights at the unload justifies going to the top of the range, not 27% past it — the origin has an elevator, it's 1,060 sqft, there's no packing, and it's a sub-one-mile haul. Worth pulling the actual against this one when it books. Also fix the differentiator naming: 'evaluation coverage' should be 'No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage,' and pair it with the 60¢/lb industry baseline so the customer understands what she's actually getting.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently courteous and easy to deal with — 'Yeah, absolutely,' 'good deal,' and a genuinely non-defensive read on both objections — but the warmth stayed procedural: no name used once, a string of bare 'Okay. Okay. Okay.' acknowledgments, and a roughly 250-word pricing monologue with no check-in that reduced the customer to 'Mm-hmm.'
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace bullet was deducted on transcript evidence alone, and that evidence is ambiguous: the pricing block runs as one long unbroken stretch with several garbled words ('stop for a launch at a gas station,' 'Fifteen minutes, Reval of what you actually needed') and the customer's replies interleave out of sequence. Audio is needed to tell whether he was genuinely rushing and running words together or whether this is transcription artifact on a fast but clear delivery.
